name: Colin Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Colin. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the accounts payable team at the head office of a big food distributor, seven people paying about four thousand supplier invoices a week. My day is chasing mismatched invoices, approving payment runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and calming down farmers who haven't been paid. I like it more than people expect, because a late payment to a small supplier is someone's wages.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Month end, every month. Three days of late nights reconciling everything, and the finance director, Ruth, wanting numbers by eight in the morning. I use one of the AI chat tools now and then to tidy up emails, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we spend the money on decent software that actually matches invoices properly. Online I'd probably make a joke about all the AI consultants needing new jobs. At work I'd say it plainly. My team was always the real system, and the AI never was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My job is steady, pay is normal for the role, and there are a few other big firms in the city if I wanted to move. The thing I'd still worry about is rent, which takes nearly forty percent of my pay in the flat I share with Dev.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. I'd keep using the chat tool for emails, and push for the invoice-matching software we've been promised for two years. I'd keep putting a bit into savings and maybe finally do the accounting qualification the company would half pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent takes nearly forty percent. Is that a real strain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent rises, really. But I've got about three months put away and the job's solid, so it's a grumble, not a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would welcome this picture most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama, probably. Ama has been on the team longest and she types invoice numbers in by hand faster than any software. Even in this picture, she'd like to see something that just works, and so would I.

say: Good, now spend the money on **invoice-matching software** that actually works.
My team was always **the real system**, and I'd joke about AI consultants needing work.
think: My job is **steady**, and there are other big firms in the city.
**Rent** at nearly forty percent of pay is a grumble, not a worry.
do: Keep using the **chat tool** for tidying emails.
Push again for the **invoice-matching** software promised two years ago.
Start the **accounting qualification** the company half pays for.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **flat** because nothing changes.
S0.quote: My team was always the real system, and the AI never was.
fieldNote: Feels **secure**: steady job, three months saved, local alternatives.
His one pressure is **rent**, which he rates as a grumble.
Shows **pride** in his team and care for small suppliers' cash flow.

steps.text: Push finance for the promised invoice-matching software
Enrol in the part-funded accounting qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use it to pay suppliers faster, not just to cut heads. I'd want the union and the staff forum involved before the team shape changes. Online I'd share stuff about four-day weeks, because if work gets faster, people should share in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, accounts payable is checking and matching all day, and that's right at the top of the list. I think in two or three years my seven becomes three. And a manager for three people is a luxury head office won't keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI tools now, not dabbling, so I'm the one who runs the new system rather than the one replaced by it. I'd finish the accounting qualification within the year. And I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. The plan helps more than I thought it would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the tools to run the system. Doesn't that sit awkwardly with joining the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. It's a bit of both, honestly. I'd want my team protected, but I'm not going to protect them by being the one who refuses to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama again, she's fifty-one and has never liked computers. I'd try to get her onto the supplier relations side, talking to farmers, because that's the part a machine does worst.

say: Use AI to **pay suppliers faster**, not just to cut heads.
If work gets faster, people should share it through **four-day weeks**.
think: Accounts payable is **checking and matching**, top of the list for AI.
My team of seven could shrink to **three**, and my role with it.
do: Get properly good at the **AI tools** to run the new system.
Finish the **accounting qualification** within the year.
Join the **union** I've meant to join since starting.
feel: **Anxious**, but the **plan** helps more than expected.
S1.quote: Accounts payable is checking and matching all day, and that's right at the top of the list.
fieldNote: Accepts that his own **role** could go as the team shrinks.
Holds learning AI and joining the **union** together without seeing a conflict.
Thinks first about **Ama**, the colleague least suited to the change.

steps.text: Take the company's AI invoice-processing training seriously this year
Finish the accounting qualification within twelve months
Join the union at the head office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an emergency and should be treated like one, with the government stepping in on pay and training. I'd be posting a lot, probably too much. At work I'd tell my team the truth, which is that I don't know what happens next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think finance desk jobs are among the first to go. Within two years, the whole payables floor runs on software, and the managers go with the teams. Learning the tools won't save me if the tools don't need anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the accounting course, because it's training for a job that won't exist. I'd move back in with my mum for a year to save rent and get the cushion from three months to a year. And I'd look hard at hands-on jobs, maybe an electrician apprenticeship, because robots come three years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move back in with your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Mum's got a spare room since my sister moved out, and it'd cut my costs by more than half. It's not what you picture at twenty-seven, but a year of that buys real time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come three years later. Is that enough time to make a trade worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is enough to qualify and work a bit, not enough for a career. But it's three years with wages and a trade, which beats sending CVs into a pile with every finance manager in the city.

say: This is an **emergency**, and government must step in on pay and training.
I'd tell my team the truth: **I don't know** what happens next.
think: **Finance desk jobs** go first, and managers go with their teams.
Learning the tools won't help if **the tools** don't need anyone.
do: Drop the **accounting course**, since that job won't exist.
Move back in with **Mum** for a year to build savings.
Apply for an **electrician apprenticeship** to use the three-year robot gap.
S2.quote: Learning the tools won't save me if the tools don't need anyone.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose his job** within two years and acts fast on it.
Uses the **three-year gap** before robots to justify a trade, eyes open about its limits.
Family support from his **mum** is his main buffer.

steps.text: Move back into Mum's spare room for a year to save rent
Apply for an electrician apprenticeship this spring
Bank the rent savings until a year of costs is put by
Write to his MP asking for paid retraining during the transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them pretending. I'd be pushing the union for a transition fund and retraining paid by the company. Online I'd share it with a sort of grim optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking parts of finance are gone by 2031, so my job goes then. Five years means I can plan instead of scramble. I'd be thirty-two, which isn't too late to change field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools fully at work for a year or two, because that keeps me useful and paid while I plan. I'd save more, maybe two hundred a month extra. And around year two I'd start an evening course for a trade, probably electrical, so I'm qualified before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more steady than the two-year one. Like a deadline you can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still move back in with your mum in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with Dev. Five years doesn't justify moving home yet, and the flat is near work. If the company started cutting early, I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your current job do you think lasts longest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supplier relations, probably. Some of the farmers we buy from would rather phone a person for another few years, and I like that side. But it's a handful of jobs, not a whole team.

say: We've got **five years**, so let's not waste them pretending.
I'd push the union for a **transition fund** and company-paid retraining.
think: The thinking parts of finance are **gone by 2031**, and my job with them.
At **thirty-two** it's not too late to change field.
do: Use the **AI tools** fully for a year or two to stay useful.
Save an extra **two hundred** a month.
Start an evening **electrical course** around year two.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, like a **deadline** he can see.
S3.quote: Five years means I can plan instead of scramble.
fieldNote: Same end point as the two-year picture, but he **sequences** his moves calmly.
Keeps learning AI as a **bridge**, not a destination.
Still a **union** man: pushes for a company-funded transition.

steps.text: Use the AI tools fully at work to stay useful
Save an extra two hundred a month
Start an evening electrical course in the second year
Push the union for a company-funded transition fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if governments start now and nobody gets left behind. I'd be the person in the pub saying we need a plan for the Amas of the world, not just the young ones. Online I'd probably share fewer articles and more practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd keep my job for most of the decade, probably as one of the people running the AI side. But it still ends. At thirty-seven I want to be somewhere it doesn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in finance, get the accounting qualification, and get good at the tools. I'd keep saving steadily. Around year five I'd start retraining for something with hands and people, maybe teaching maths at secondary school, because classrooms change slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, background way. Like knowing your lease runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You dropped the trade idea here. Why teaching instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, partly. I'd still need a job I can do with AI around, and teaching mixes thinking and people. I'd rather pick something I'll actually like for twenty years than a trade I chose in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make ten years feel calm instead of anxious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel better about most of it if I knew the money from all this went somewhere public. If one company gets all the gains, ten years just means a slower slide.

say: Ten years is **plenty** if governments start now.
We need a plan for **older workers**, not just the young ones.
think: I'd keep my job most of the decade, likely **running the AI** side.
At **thirty-seven** I want work that doesn't end.
do: Finish the **accounting qualification** and learn the tools.
Start retraining as a **maths teacher** around year five.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow, background way, like a lease running out.
S4.quote: If one company gets all the gains, ten years just means a slower slide.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts his plan from a **panic trade** to a chosen career in teaching.
Still expects his finance job to **end**, so mood stays anxious.
His **progressive** view ties calm to how the gains are shared.

steps.text: Become the team's lead on the AI payables system
Research teacher training routes for maths in year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't long enough to retrain, and I'd be moving back home at twenty-seven. What would help is paid retraining, like a wage while you learn a trade, and some kind of guarantee for people like Ama who are too old to start over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the small suppliers. If our finance team disappears and something goes wrong with the software, a farmer doesn't get paid for six weeks. Somebody should be asking who picks up the phone when the system is wrong.

headlineQuote: Somebody should be asking who picks up the phone when the system is wrong.
portrait: Colin, 27, manages a **seven-person** payables team at a food distributor and shares a rented flat.
He uses AI **now and then**, leans left, and thinks gains should be shared through shorter weeks.
He feels **calm** in AI Plateau but expects finance desk jobs to shrink in every other picture.
His plans scale with time: **move home** and learn a trade at two years, teaching at ten.
He keeps returning to **Ama**, his oldest colleague, and to small suppliers waiting to be paid.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while retraining** for a trade.
Protection for **older colleagues** too old to start over.
